summary: Defines how to use the Diffie-Hellman algorithms X25519 and X448 and the signature algorithms Ed25519 and Ed448 in JOSE, the JSON-based signing and encryption framework.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets the JSON signing and encryption framework use the newer cryptographic curves. It adds one new kind of key, called OKP, for keys that are just strings of bytes, and it names the new signature algorithm so that software can recognise it.

subtitle: How JOSE carries the modern X25519, X448, Ed25519 and Ed448 algorithms: one new key type and one new signature name.

tldr.problem: JOSE, the JSON-based framework for signing and encryption, had no way to use the newer elliptic curve algorithms that the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group had chosen, because those algorithms work on raw byte strings rather than on the point formats JOSE already knew.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new JSON Web Key type, "OKP", for octet string key pairs, and registers the signature algorithm name "EdDSA" with the key subtypes Ed25519 and Ed448, alongside the ECDH-ES key subtypes X25519 and X448.
tldr.outcome: The result is that JOSE documents and libraries can carry the modern curves without pretending they sit on a named elliptic curve. RFC 8037 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 8037 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9864. The OKP key type and the EdDSA, Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448 names it registered are the ones still used for these algorithms in JOSE.

sections.title: Bringing the New Curves to JOSE
sections.content:
The IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) selected new Diffie-Hellman algorithms, X25519 and X448, and new signature algorithms, Ed25519 and Ed448, for asymmetric key cryptography. This document defines how to use those algorithms in JOSE in an interoperable manner, following the conventions used in the context of RFC 7515, RFC 7516 and RFC 7517.

One design decision is worth spelling out. The CFRG also defined two pairs of isogenous elliptic curves that underlie these algorithms, but those curves are not directly exposed, because the algorithms laid on top are sufficient for the purposes of JOSE and are much easier to use.

All inputs to and outputs from the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and signature functions are defined to be octet strings, with the exception of the outputs of verification functions, which are booleans.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer curves do arithmetic on raw byte strings, so they do not fit the shape JOSE expected of a curve key. This RFC says how to wrap them so that everything still fits.

sections.title: The OKP Key Type
sections.content:
A new key type value, kty of "OKP" for Octet Key Pair, is defined for public key algorithms that use octet strings as private and public keys. It has four parameters. The parameter kty MUST be "OKP". The parameter crv MUST be present and contain the subtype of the key, taken from the "JSON Web Elliptic Curve" registry. The parameter x MUST be present and contain the public key encoded using the base64url encoding. The parameter d MUST be present for private keys and contain the private key encoded using the base64url encoding, and MUST NOT be present for public keys.

The RFC adds a warning that is easy to miss. Do not assume that there is an underlying elliptic curve, despite the existence of the crv and x parameters. The key type could be extended to represent Diffie-Hellman algorithms based on hyperelliptic surfaces, for example.

One more rule concerns thumbprints. When calculating JWK Thumbprints as described in RFC 7638, the three public key fields are included in the hash input in lexicographic order: crv, kty and x.
sections.plainLanguage: A key of this kind is three or four strings: the kind of key, which variant it is, the public bytes and, for a private key, the private bytes. The thumbprint that identifies a key is computed from the three public ones, in a fixed order.

sections.title: EdDSA Signatures
sections.content:
For the purpose of using the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) for signing data with the JSON Web Signature format, the algorithm name "EdDSA" is defined, to be applied as the value of the alg parameter. Two key subtypes are defined for use with EdDSA: the curve name "Ed25519" for the Ed25519 variant and "Ed448" for the Ed448 variant. The key type used with these keys is "OKP" and the algorithm used for signing is "EdDSA".

These subtypes MUST NOT be used for Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static (ECDH-ES). The EdDSA variant used is determined by the subtype of the key.

Signing is performed by applying the signing algorithm defined in RFC 8032 to the private key, the public key and the JWS Signing Input, which is the message. The resulting signature is the JWS Signature. Verification is performed by applying the verification algorithm of RFC 8032 to the public key, the JWS Signing Input and the signature. All inputs and outputs are octet strings. If the algorithm accepts, the signature is valid; otherwise it is invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing works exactly as it does in the original specification of these curves. The only new thing is the name that goes in the algorithm field of the document, so that a receiver knows which curve was used.

sections.title: ECDH-ES Key Agreement
sections.content:
Two key subtypes are defined for the purpose of Key Agreement with Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Static (ECDH-ES): the curve name "X25519" for the X25519 function and "X448" for the X448 function. The key type used with these keys is "OKP", and these subtypes MUST NOT be used for signing. Section 4.6 of RFC 7518 defines the ECDH-ES algorithms "ECDH-ES+A128KW", "ECDH-ES+A192KW", "ECDH-ES+A256KW" and "ECDH-ES".

Performing the ECDH operation has two halves. The "x" parameter of the ephemeral public key is set by applying the appropriate ECDH function to the ephemeral private key as scalar input and the standard base point as u-coordinate input; the base64url encoding of the output is the value for the "x" parameter of the epk field. The Z value, the raw key agreement output used in the subsequent Key Derivation Function as per Section 4.6.2 of RFC 7518, is determined by applying the appropriate ECDH function to the ephemeral private key as scalar input and the receiver's public key as u-coordinate input. All inputs and outputs are octet strings.
sections.plainLanguage: For key agreement the sender makes up a temporary key pair, puts the public half in the message, and combines it with the recipient's public key to get a shared secret. The shared secret is then stretched into the encryption key by the usual JOSE derivation function.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations from RFC 7748 and RFC 8032 apply.

The RFC then adds rules of its own. Do not separate key material from information about what key subtype it is for: when using keys, check that the algorithm is compatible with the key subtype for the key, because doing otherwise opens the system up to attacks that mix up algorithms. It is particularly dangerous to mix up signature and Message Authentication Code (MAC) algorithms.

Although for Ed25519 and Ed448 the signature binds the key used for signing, do not assume this in general, because there are many signature algorithms that fail to make such a binding. If key binding is desired, include the key used for signing either inside the JWS protected header or in the data to sign.

If key generation or batch signature verification is performed, a well-seeded cryptographic random number generator is REQUIRED. Signing and non-batch signature verification are deterministic operations and do not need random numbers of any kind.

Two further points concern key agreement. The JWA ECDH-ES KDF construction does not mix keys into the final shared secret. In key exchange such mixing could be a bad mistake, whereas here either the receiver's public key has to be chosen maliciously or the sender has to be malicious in order to cause problems, and in either case all security evaporates. The nominal security strengths of X25519 and X448 are about 126 and about 223 bits, so using 256-bit symmetric encryption, especially key wrapping and encryption, with X448 is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the algorithm and the key type matched, or an attacker may try to use one in place of the other. And because X448 is stronger than X25519, the RFC recommends the larger symmetric key when you use it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Four registries are extended. The "JSON Web Key Types" registry gains the kty value "OKP", described as octet string key pairs, with JOSE implementation requirements Optional and the change controller IESG. The "JSON Web Key Parameters" registry gains three parameters: "crv", the subtype of key pair, which is public and used with the "OKP" key type; "d", the private key, which is private and used with "OKP"; and "x", the public key, which is public and used with "OKP".

The "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms" registry gains the algorithm name "EdDSA", for EdDSA signature algorithms, with usage location "alg" and JOSE implementation requirements Optional. The "JSON Web Elliptic Curve" registry gains four curve names: "Ed25519" and "Ed448", described as signature algorithm key pairs, and "X25519" and "X448", described as function key pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the lists of key types, key parameters, algorithms and curve names. This RFC adds the new key type, its parameters, the new signature name and the four curve names.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A works through a complete example, using material taken from the test vectors of RFC 7748 and RFC 8032 wherever possible.

The first example is an Ed25519 private key as a JSON Web Key, with the kind "OKP", the curve "Ed25519", the private key in the "d" parameter and the public key in the "x" parameter. The second example is the public part of that key, which simply omits "d". The third example is the thumbprint canonicalization of those two, which is the three public fields in the order crv, kty and x, with a line break inserted for formatting. The RFC gives the SHA-256 hash of that canonicalization in hexadecimal and the resulting base64url encoded thumbprint.

The fourth example signs a message. The protected header is {"alg":"EdDSA"} and the payload is the text "Example of Ed25519 signing". The JWS signing input is the concatenation of the base64url encoding of the header, a dot, and the base64url encoding of the payload. Applying the Ed25519 signing algorithm with the private key, the public key and that signing input yields a signature, which the RFC gives in hexadecimal and then in base64url. The compact serialization of the JWS is the signing input, a dot, and the base64url encoding of the signature. The fifth example verifies the same JWS: it has two dots in it, the base64url decoding of the protected header yields {"alg":"EdDSA"}, and since the key has the kind "OKP" and the curve "Ed25519", it is an Ed25519 signature. Applying the Ed25519 verification algorithm to the public key, the signing input and the signature yields true, so the signature is valid.

Two more examples cover key agreement, with ECDH-ES over X25519 and over X448.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix carries the whole thing through: a key, its thumbprint, a signed message and a check that the signature is good. The values come from the published test vectors of the two curve documents.
